findings.what: "Read √−4 as j2 ... and √−9 as j3" is the first time a √ of a negative appears, and no earlier screen says that j is what people call the square root of −1, or that j3, which squares to −9, is therefore read as √−9. That is a skipped step. One sentence on screen 8's why or screen 9's text would close it.

The brief promised that one screen would show both views: mathcentre defines j = √−1 and gets j² = −1 from it, while Scimath leads with j² = −1. That point is only in explain.text, which a steps lesson does not show on the lesson screen, and the JSON has contested: null and confidence: "settled". So on the screens Dan reads, the contested point is not taught as contested.

The brief promised a screen saying that maths books, Khan, Brilliant and HELM write i for the same number, and that engineers write j because i is current (DSPRelated, source 4). That is only in explain.text, so in the lesson itself Dan meets j without being told why his college maths texts write i.
The right answer is j3 alone, but the lesson's own common mistakes call giving one answer to x² = −9 a slip. Offer ±j3, as screen 13 does with ±j2, or ask for "one number that" answers it.
"Stretch the arrow to 3, then turn it" reads as an instruction, but this screen has no stretch or turn control, only three answers. Say that after Check the arrow stretches to 3 and turns.

findings.where: Screens 8, 9, 10 and 13 (number-line views B and D, 15 and 11 px per unit)
findings.what: The opening arrow from 0 to 1 is barely longer than its own head. In the 360 px end shot of screen 13 it looks like a mark on the 0 tick, so the thing that will turn cannot be seen before Check. Label its tip 1 or draw it heavier.
The tick labels −16, −12, −4, 0, 4, 8 skip −8, which looks like a missing label, and at 360 px a wide blank band sits between the task and the line.
After Check, a wrong pick (45° or 180°) is drawn in ink, the same as the right one, while every other puzzle draws a slip's motion in red. Draw the slip's arrows and trace in red here too.

"That arrow points straight down: it is −j" gives no reason. Add that straight down is j turned half round, −1 × j = −j; screen 6 gives this reason later, for j³. The screen also packs j and −j into one dense paragraph.

The task assumes, without saying so, that the new number will also act as a turn. One clause such as "Suppose the new number turns arrows too" would make the guess honest before the handle shows that it works.
The text gives b = 2 and c = 5 but not a = 1, though the ÷ 2 comes from 2a. The picture also has no j label on the up direction, so the place of −1 + j2 is not tied back to screen 5's j.

Two things the brief listed for lesson 1 appear on no screen: the general form a + jb, and the word "imaginary" as a word to notice (the j part of an impedance can be measured). Screen 11 could carry both in one line.
On this SHOW screen the ring at −9 and the line "x × x = −9 → no answer on the line" are red, though nothing is a mistake. Red is kept for slips, and screen 2 marks the same target with an ink ring.

findings.where: Source caption under the frame, 360 px
findings.what: "j²" and "= −1 (mathcentre)" break across two lines. Keep j² = −1 together with nowrap.

"Each number drawn as an arrow from 0 on a number line, and three example equations" takes four lines above every screen at 360 px, and it does not describe screens 1-2, which show two number lines with dots. Shorten it.
The lesson column and its small picture sit in the left third of a full-width card, with the other two thirds blank. Centre the column or let the scene grow on desktop.

The breaks is true, but it undersells the analogy. Turning a phasor 90° is exactly what multiplying by j does in lessons 5-8, so it is worth saying that the analogy becomes exact once the wave is drawn as its arrow.
